Whenever I see people getting excited about zHBM, it reminds me of when I first started graduate school.

One of our lab’s first government-funded research projects was on 3D IC technology, and my part was studying the testing standard, IEEE 1838. Back then, I remember having intense discussions with senior researchers about when heterogeneous 3D ICs would ever become a reality, from thermal issues to all the other technical challenges that came with them.

You know what’s funny?

When I interviewed for an SK hynix industry scholarship in 2017, one of the questions they asked me was:

“How can SK hynix catch up with Samsung Electronics in memory?”

I answered based on what I had been studying and talked about the concept of 3D ICs. At the time, I didn’t even know the term HBM very well, so I could only explain the idea in fairly abstract terms.

The response I got from the interviewer was:

“I think you need to study more.”

Looking back at those moments now, it’s kind of amazing how much has changed without me even realizing it.

SK hynix actually did catch up with Samsung Electronics.

And heterogeneous 3D ICs have now been introduced to the world under the somewhat funny name of zHBM.

It makes me genuinely curious and excited to see what other technologies we talk about today as distant possibilities will eventually become reality.
Looks like SK hynix isn’t working with Intel on the HBM base die after all. 🫡

When I look at $BE, what interests me is not the growth rate of the fuel-cell market itself.

One of the biggest constraints on new AI data centers in the US is power. You can secure the GPUs and build the campus, but getting large amounts of power from the grid can still take 3–6 years.

In that environment, even if onsite power is more expensive, the economics can still make sense if it lets you bring the data center online years earlier.

That is why I think Bloom’s first Oracle deployment being completed in just 55 days matters.

The role of onsite generation is not simply to replace grid power. It is to separate the construction schedule of an AI campus from the grid interconnection schedule.

And if this model scales, the bottleneck shifts.

Today, the question is how quickly you can get connected to the grid.

Tomorrow, it may be how quickly you can manufacture and deploy the generation equipment itself.

I see 800 VDC in the same context.

800 VDC helps you run more GPUs within the power you already have.

Onsite generation helps you secure that power much earlier in the first place.

The broader direction is simple:

AI infrastructure is trying to stop letting the pace of GPU deployment be dictated by the pace of traditional power infrastructure.

That is why I see Bloom less as a simple fuel-cell growth story, and more as a new infrastructure layer emerging as AI data centers look for ways around the grid bottleneck.

If Rubin CPX is really coming back with these specs, the investment takeaway is not just that NVIDIA is adding another GPU. It is that the inference BOM gets structurally larger.

The old CPX used GDDR7. The revived version reportedly moves to 168GB of HBM4 and is designed to pair with Rubin at roughly a 1:1 ratio.

CPX = Prefill + KV-cache creation
Rubin = Decode

The KV cache then moves between the two pools over Ethernet RDMA. NVLink is used only within the 8-GPU tray, while the rest of the system scales through Spectrum-6 Ethernet and OSFP optics.

That makes HBM the most direct read-through.

A Rubin GPU carries 288GB of HBM4. Adding a 168GB CPX alongside it increases total HBM capacity per paired inference system by roughly 58% versus Rubin alone. Since the previous CPX used GDDR7, this would represent incremental HBM demand that was not in the old design.

So the first sector I would watch is HBM: SK hynix, Samsung, and Micron.

The second is optics.

Once prefill and decode are separated into different GPU pools, the system has to move KV cache and context between them. If that traffic runs across OSFP optical links, inference disaggregation itself creates additional scale-out optical demand.

That makes Lumentum and Coherent worth watching.

The third is power and cooling.

If a 2,300W-class CPX is deployed alongside Rubin at close to a 1:1 ratio, the architecture may improve cost per token while still driving much higher absolute power density and MW demand.

That keeps Vertiv and the broader AI power infrastructure stack relevant.

So my current order of interest would be:

HBM → Optics → Power/Cooling

The bigger point is simple.

Splitting prefill and decode does not just add another accelerator. It creates a second memory pool and a network between the two.

NVIDIA is turning inference from a GPU problem into a much larger system BOM opportunity.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics has raised OEM MLCC prices. AI server-grade X6S pricing is reportedly up around 10–20% depending on the customer, while consumer-grade X5R has seen a larger increase of roughly 25–30%.

What I find more interesting than the price hike itself is why the consumer side was raised more aggressively.

This looks less like a broad passive-component upcycle and more like an attempt to push out lower-value consumer demand and free up capacity for higher-value server MLCCs.

In AI servers, MLCCs act as local charge buffers near the chip, helping stabilize voltage as GPUs and ASICs draw enormous current. As power density rises, this function becomes more important.

Even if NVIDIA brings more of the infrastructure stack in-house, including NVLink, networking, optics, and memory interfaces, this function does not disappear. The same applies to AMD and hyperscaler custom ASICs.

So when looking at AI infrastructure, it is important to track not only what NVIDIA internalizes, but also which functions remain structurally dependent on external suppliers.

MLCCs are one of them.

And that makes Murata, which already has a strong position in high-capacitance server MLCCs, worth watching closely. If Japanese suppliers also begin raising prices, that would suggest this is no longer just Samsung Electro-Mechanics optimizing its product mix, but a broader sign that pricing power is strengthening across high-end MLCCs.

What I find most interesting about the Saudi HUMAIN deployment of AMD MI355X is not AMD itself, but the networking socket Cisco is capturing.

The production system does not use an NVIDIA-style NVLink rack-scale scale-up fabric.

Within each node, the GPUs are connected through AMD Infinity Fabric, while the backend network that connects nodes and racks is built around Cisco Silicon One-based Ethernet and 800G-class pluggable optics.

In other words, the infrastructure generating actual traffic and revenue in 2026 is not yet the scale-up NPO/CPO laser stack, but Cisco’s AI Ethernet stack.

If this architecture becomes a common deployment template for sovereign AI, it could become quite meaningful for Cisco.

More broadly, when looking at AI infrastructure, I think it is increasingly important to study not only NVIDIA’s roadmap, but also the architecture being built outside the NVIDIA ecosystem.

NVIDIA is steadily extending its control beyond GPUs into NVLink, NVSwitch, networking, optics, memory interfaces, and more layers of the overall infrastructure stack.

Customers that choose not to use NVIDIA still need all of those functions to be provided by someone else.

If they deploy AMD accelerators, the questions become: who provides the scale-up fabric, who supplies the scale-out switches, which NICs and optics are used, and who defines the memory and rack architecture?

As NVIDIA becomes more vertically integrated, it will become increasingly important for investors to identify who is building the alternative AI infrastructure stack on the other side.

But in the end, it just started to feel like another generic news summary that anyone could make.

Seoul Economic Daily, citing Korea International Trade Association figures released on the 31st, says AI-related DRAM is getting scarcer even as the export bill keeps rising. Export volumes of DRAM used in AI chips, including HBM and LPDDR, fell 13.2% to 591.74 million units in July from about 681.70 million units in May. Total DRAM export value still rose 18.5% to $13.55 billion from $11.43 billion, and the average unit price jumped 36.6% to $22.90 from $16.76.

The paper says expanding HBM4 shipments to customers such as Nvidia have absorbed DRAM supply. HBM4 is still in early mass production and has lower yields than HBM3E, so more DRAM is consumed per good stack. Ahn Ki-hyun, executive director of the Korea Semiconductor Industry Association, said HBM tends to see yields fall with each new generation, and that HBM4 sells for roughly twice as much as the previous generation, so as makers ramp, DRAM consumption rises and total export volumes shrink.

Samsung and SK hynix, which together account for about 70% of the global memory market according to the article, have shifted sales toward long-term agreements. Industry sources told SEDAILY that Samsung’s memory division has allocated about 70% of production capacity through 2031 to LTA volumes, with counterparties including Nvidia, Microsoft, and Google. Even those customers are not getting all of the contracted volume. MegaGrid Supply, cited by the paper, puts a 36GB HBM3E product at $2,100 (about 2.87 million won) on the spot market, four to five times the long-term contract price of roughly 500,000 to 700,000 won. A 16-layer HBM4 product being prepared for mass production trades at $3,500, or about 4.80 million won, on the spot market.

Samsung DS executives are reviewing a plan to convert S5, the only foundry line at Pyeongtaek, into memory as early as next year. Analysts compiled by SEDAILY over the past month put Samsung’s third-quarter consensus at 206.64 trillion won in revenue and 116.38 trillion won in operating profit, versus 171.50 trillion and 89.49 trillion in the second quarter. SK hynix is projected at 101.76 trillion won in revenue, up 28.2% from the prior quarter, and 79.16 trillion won in operating profit, up 30.7%. Ahn said that even once planned new plants come online, the shortage will be eased rather than eliminated.

Long-term contracts give hyperscalers a price far below the spot print, and leave the leftover spot market as an expensive overflow valve. That is why HBM can look sold out in the contract book while 36GB HBM3E still clears at four to five times the LTA. Conventional DRAM is also being pulled into HBM4’s worse early yields, which shows up as falling unit exports and a 36.6% jump in DRAM unit price. Converting Pyeongtaek S5 from foundry to memory is a memory-over-foundry choice.

The Public, citing electrical-industry figures as of the 26th, says AI-server demand has pushed Korean package-substrate lines close to a full run-rate. Samsung Electro-Mechanics’ semiconductor package-substrate utilization was 89% in the first half. LG Innotek produced 437,000 sheets against capacity of 465,000, or 94% utilization. FC-BGA is the substrate that connects high-performance CPUs and GPUs to the motherboard. As AI accelerators get larger and carry more HBM, the substrate has to get bigger and more layered, and new lines take a long time to stand up.

Samsung Electro-Mechanics president Jang Duk-hyun said after the March shareholders’ meeting that server and data-center FC-BGA demand is more than 50% above production capacity. That tightness is already in the P&L. First-half package-substrate average selling price at Samsung Electro-Mechanics rose 18.7% from a year earlier. Package Solution sales were 1.4966 trillion won, up 41%, and operating profit was 160.2 billion won, up 237%. LG Innotek’s Package Solution first-half sales were 935.6 billion won, up 18%, and operating profit was 99.6 billion won, up 94%.

The paper notes that as Nvidia moves the Vera Rubin platform into volume, the package that ties GPU and HBM together gets more complex, so adding GPU and HBM output without matching high-spec substrates can still stall accelerator shipments. Samsung Electro-Mechanics plans 8 trillion won at Sejong and 15 trillion won at Busan through 2040, plus 1.8 trillion won for FC-BGA in Vietnam. LG Innotek is putting 1.6 trillion won into Gumi and Vietnam substrate capacity and building a new plant in Haiphong.

Sourcing HBM4E base dies from Intel would be much harder for SK hynix than it sounds.

The biggest issue is ecosystem portability. Custom HBM base dies can include customer-specific and third-party IP that has already been validated on TSMC’s PDK, libraries, SRAM, PHYs, PLLs, and I/O. Moving to Intel could therefore require IP porting, physical re-implementation, sign-off, silicon validation, and customer re-qualification.

The economics are also more complicated than wafer price. What matters is cost per qualified good die after additional NRE, yield learning, packaging integration, and qualification. The current accelerator packaging ecosystem is also heavily tied to TSMC CoWoS.

Most importantly, the customer has to agree to use the Intel-based version.

So the real question is not whether Intel can manufacture the base die. It is whether the entire customer/IP/package ecosystem can be ported to Intel economically and qualified again. That is much harder.

A lot of people are now talking about NVHBM and repeating the importance of custom HBM and logic dies as if these were new discoveries.

They are not.

The industry has been discussing these concepts for the past two to three years. Simply repeating them does not add much value.

That is not what this article is about.

The real questions are: Where do memory companies ultimately want to go? What are NVIDIA and other hyperscaler customers trying to prevent? And if this power structure is changing, which parts of the value chain should investors actually be watching?

Technical facts alone are not investment insight.

The value comes from understanding the incentives, the conflicts, and the strategic implications behind those facts, then translating them into investable ideas.

That is exactly the kind of research I want to do.
